newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU says Boeing offers not good enough.
newsitem.headline: EU says Boeing offers not good enough.

text.p: The European Commission said Tuesday that Boeing Co. had so far failed to address its competition concerns regarding the merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp. and that it fully backed the tough stance being taken by its antitrust chief.
"Boeing has so far not agreed to measures which would meet these concerns and achieve that objective," the commission said in a statement.
The statement was the strongest indication to date from the commission that it may block the $14 billion merger at its next weekly meeting July 23.

"Unless the legitimate competition concerns of the commission can be met and genuine choice maintained for purchasers of aircraft worldwide, the commission could not approve the merger," the written statement by commission spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas said.

Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has expressed fears that the deal would strengthen Boeing's dominant position in the civil aviation market, although McDonnell Douglas has become a minor player.
Antitrust experts from the 15 EU countries agreed unanimously July 4 that the deal could not be allowed if the commission's competition concerns were not addressed.
If Boeing went ahead with the deal regardless of the decision, the commission could fine it up to 10 percent of revenue and also fine any European companies that did business with it.

The commission originally gave Boeing a deadline of midnight Monday night, Brussels time, to alleviate the commission's concerns about its effects on competition. But the talks went on into the night, and when they broke up, it gave Boeing more time ahead of a final deadline on July 23.
The commission has expressed concerns about the merger's impact on competition in three areas, arguing, for example, that it would add to Boeing's already dominant position in the aircraft industry.

It also opposes Boeing's exclusive contracts to supply aircraft to airlines such as Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Continental Airlines and worries about the possibility of spillovers of government money, earmarked for research and development in defence, into Boeing's civil aviation business.
Although McDonnell Douglas has become a minor player in the civil aviation sector, the commission is also concerned that the deal will increase Boeing's customer base.

About 25 percent of all planes in the world's fleets are McDonnell's, and the commission fears Boeing will somehow tie the servicing and maintenance of those planes to their replacement by its own aircraft. It also sees McDonnell's spare parts business as a lucrative addition to Boeing's business.

The commission has been in new talks with the United States since the beginning of the year on better enforcement of a 1992 bilateral agreement on controlling aircraft subsidies amid European accusations that the United States is not respecting the deal.
